Account Enumeration Lab — one external address, twenty usernames, one success
  1 / 1
Start●

You have been handed an alert. Work out what happened.

no experience needed~75 min

A security alert fired overnight. Your job is to decide one thing: is this a real attack that must be escalated, or a false alarm that can be closed?

You will answer it the way a real analyst does — not by guessing, but by running the evidence in order and writing down what you find as you go. By the last card you will know exactly which address did it, when, against which server, which account it took, and why that account was not a lucky guess.

What this guide is

It starts at zeroNo security knowledge, no Elastic experience. If you can double-click a file, you can do this lab.
Every picture is realNot a drawing. Each one is a screenshot of this exact lab, so the words, the tabs and the numbers are the product’s own.
It tells you what to expectAfter every action it states the number or the text your screen must now be showing. Compare, and you cannot go wrong.

The one thing you need first

Docker Desktop, installed and running. That is the only prerequisite. The lab runs inside it and installs nothing else on your computer. If you do not have Docker Desktop yet, ask your instructor — this lab assumes it is already there.

Prep1

The words you need to know

read once

You will see all of these in the tool and in your report. Read them once now and the rest of the lab becomes much easier.

The pieces

AlertA rule that fires when something looks dangerous. It is a hint, not a fact. It might be nothing at all.
ElasticsearchThe database that stores and searches the logs. Answers web addresses like localhost:9200.
KibanaThe website you do all the work in, on top of Elasticsearch. Lives at localhost:5601.
IndexOne named pile of log records of the same shape. Ours are auth-* and network-*.
Data viewKibana’s word for “which pile shall I look at”. Older versions called it an index pattern.
DocumentOne single log record. There are 280 in the auth pile. This is what you read.
FieldOne labelled box inside a document, like source.ip. The part before the dot is the group.
TimestampThe @timestamp field — when it happened. Everything in this lab is stored in UTC.
KQLThe query language Kibana speaks. field: value means “field equals value”, and and joins two conditions.
IOCIndicator of Compromise — evidence that something bad happened, e.g. an address, an account, a process name.
Rows per pageThe control at the bottom left of the results. It is set to 100 in this lab, so a result set of 20 fits on one screen.

The two attacks this lab is about

Brute forceTry many passwords against one account, fast. It normally trips the account lockout within minutes and sets off alarms.
Username enumerationTry one password against many accounts, slowly, one each. No account is ever tried twice, so nothing ever locks.
Rejection statusWindows records why a logon failed. “No such user” means the name was a guess; “wrong password” means the account is real. That is the attacker’s feedback channel.
LockoutAfter enough failures Windows locks the account — event 4740. It is the defender’s automatic defence, and attackers pace themselves to stay under it.

The three fields that matter most

Almost every question in this investigation is answered by three fields. Learn these and the rest of the lab is just typing:

  • event.code — the number of the Windows log record. It tells you what kind of thing happened. You only need four:
    4625 = logon failed  ·  4624 = logon succeeded  ·  4740 = account locked out  ·  4688 = a program was started
  • source.ip — the address the attempt came from. This is the field to pivot on in this lab.
  • host.name — the server the attempt was made against, which is the machine the attacker was aiming at, not the machine identifying him.
The shape of the attack, before you see it

Enumeration is quiet. Twenty failed logons, one per account, evenly spaced, from one outside address — and then, seventeen minutes after the last one, a single success for an account that had just been probed. Hold that picture in your head. By the middle of this lab you will be hunting for it, and the hunt is what turns an alert into a verdict.

Start the lab — one file

first run is slowthen wait

The lab is a real Elastic Stack running on your own computer, hidden behind one file that does all the work. You start it once; it loads everything for you, builds the alert, and checks its own homework.

Do this

  1. Open the lab folder — the folder that contains this guide.
  2. On Windows, find the file called setup-lab.cmd and double-click it.
    On macOS or Linux, open a terminal in this folder and run ./setup-lab.sh instead.
    They are the same lab. Whichever one you run, it names every object after this folder, and the other script picks up exactly where it left off.
  3. A command window opens and starts downloading Elasticsearch and Kibana. Do not close it.
  4. Wait until it prints The lab is ready. and the two addresses. This is the slow part: 5 to 20 minutes the very first time, under a minute afterwards.
  5. Your web browser opens by itself at the end, on the Alerts page. That is the next card.
Two things to type, once, when it finishes

The lab's Kibana has security switched on, so the browser will ask who you are. The account is lab_kibana and the password is LabKibana001. They are throwaway lab credentials that protect nothing, and the browser remembers you for the rest of the lab. The setup file also prints them, and prints the curl form -u lab_kibana:LabKibana001 for when you want to check the cluster by hand.

Why security is on at all: a detection rule cannot be created against a cluster with security disabled, so without it the Alerts page would be permanently empty and this lab would have no alert to investigate.

The one thing that stops most people

Docker Desktop must be installed and running. The lab runs both programs inside Docker containers. If setup-lab.cmd says docker was not found, or that it is installed but not running, open Docker Desktop, wait until it says Engine running, then run the file again. That one check fixes almost every startup problem.

What you should see

A black window that works through numbered stages, ending with this:

The last thing the setup file prints The lab is ready. Elasticsearch : http://127.0.0.1:9200 Kibana : http://127.0.0.1:5601 data view "auth" index pattern auth-* data view "network" index pattern network-* The stack has security switched on, so there are two things to type. They are lab credentials. They protect nothing. Kibana login lab_kibana / LabKibana001 in curl -u lab_kibana:LabKibana001

Just above that it prints the seven investigation queries together with the number each one must return, and the number of alerts on the Alerts page. Keep that list: it is your reference sheet, and every one of those numbers is checked again in the last card of this guide — by the setup file itself, against the live index, before it let you start.

What it did for you while you waited

So the output does not frighten you, the script performed exactly the four jobs that would otherwise be the hard part of this lab, and it verified each one:

  • Started two programs — Elasticsearch (the database) and Kibana (the website).
  • Taught Elasticsearch what each field means. An index template declares “source.ip holds a network address” and “event.code holds a number” before any data arrives. Without it Elasticsearch guesses, and guessing quietly breaks your searches.
  • Loaded 280 + 140 log records and then re-counted them, so a half-finished import can never pass as a good one.
  • Created your two data views and read them back to prove the index pattern was stored. An empty pattern matches nothing, and the symptom — no fields, no results, no visible cause — is the most confusing failure mode there is. It is now impossible.
  • Installed the detection rule and waited for it to actually fire, so the Alerts page is not empty when you arrive. A rule that has not fired yet is the single most common way a lab like this turns into a dead end.
  • Read every number in this guide back out of the running index — all seven query counts, both document totals, and the alert count — and refused to finish if any of them disagreed. The last card of this deck is that list.
  • Refused to touch a cluster it did not create, and refused to destroy a copy of this lab folder living somewhere else. If you ever see either of those messages, the script stopped rather than guessed.

A warning it prints before you start, and you will meet it again in card 7

Every time in this lab is stored in UTC, but Kibana prints timestamps in your own computer’s timezone, and the time picker does not change that. So: set the picker to UTC so the row counts are right, then read the clock times off your own screen and write down what you see. Judge the gaps between times, never the absolute numbers — a timezone shift moves every time by the same amount, so it cannot change a conclusion.

Already started it twice?

Completely safe. The script counts what is already there and skips the import. Your data will not load twice — which matters, because duplicate documents would double every count in the rest of this guide and ruin your findings. If the count is between zero and the expected number it refuses to carry on and tells you to run setup-lab.cmd reset, rather than quietly creating duplicates.

If you get a sign-in screen instead

This lab’s Kibana has security switched on, so it asks who you are once. The account is lab_kibana and the password is LabKibana001. They are throwaway lab credentials that protect nothing. Sign in and carry on — the browser remembers you for the rest of the lab.

What you are looking at

Do this

  1. Read the Severity levels table: one row, High, count 20.
  2. Read the ring in the middle. It says 20 alerts. That is twenty separate events, not one summary.
  3. Read the Alerts by name row: the rule is Slow username enumeration from a single external source, followed by a successful administrative logon, and its count is 20. Write that number down.
  4. Scroll down to the alert table underneath. Find the Reason column and read one row. It names the source address 203.0.113.45 and the account the attempt was for.
  5. Open one alert: in the first column, called Actions, click the first small icon — the two arrows pointing outwards.

What one alert says

Two different times, and the difference matters

Every alert carries two clocks, and only one of them is about the attack. @timestamp is when Elastic noticed — the day you ran the setup file, so it is a different date for every batch. kibana.alert.original_time is when the activity actually happened, and it never moves: for this lab it runs 02:20:00 to 02:58:00 on 22 September 2026.

You can see them yourself. Click the JSON tab on the alert you have open and search the text for original_time. You will find both clocks, and only one of them is the night of the attack.

The two timestamps, from one alert of this lab@timestamp the day YOU ran this kibana.alert.original_time 02:20:00 to 02:58:00, 22 Sep 2026

Which one goes in your report? The original time. Every time you write in this lab, write the time of the activity, never the time the tool noticed it. This is how every real SOC works, because logs often arrive late and rules are routinely run against history; if alerts were dated by the event, today’s genuine alerts would be buried under a wall of old ones.

The rule that fired

Worth seeing, because the rule and your own investigation are the same filter.

  1. Open the hamburger menu (☰) in the top left, then Security, then Rules. Ours is the only rule you have, so it sits under Custom rules in the list. Older builds call the page Detection rules.
  2. Tick the rule's checkbox on the left, then click the All actions button at the far right of its row and choose Edit rule settings.
  3. Scroll down to Custom query and read it.
Why this card is worth four minutes

Because it means the alert count and your own query count have to agree. The rule says 20, so when Query 3 later returns 20 you have not merely found the same answer twice — you have found the same answer the monitoring system found, by a different road. If the two numbers ever disagree, one of them is wrong, and now you know which one to trust.

If the table is empty, it is the time picker

Not a broken lab. An alert is stamped with the time it was raised, so the range this page starts on — Today, meaning from midnight — stops covering it once you cross midnight. Click the time picker at the top right, switch to the Relative tab, and set it to 1 unit Days. The twenty alerts come back. Some versions put a ready-made Last 24 hours button there instead, which does the same job. The lab itself never changed.

What you should have now

One rule, twenty High alerts, risk score 75, every one of them raised against a failed logon from 203.0.113.45 for a different account. You have not run a single query yet and you already know the shape of the attack: one outside address, twenty different usernames, no passwords, and no lockout anywhere.

What the alert does not tell you is the most important thing of all — whether any of it worked. That is what the rest of this guide is for.

Your browser just opened. Here is where you are.

no typing needed

You have read your alert. The setup file opened Kibana on the Alerts page, so come to Discover now: click the hamburger menu (☰) in the top left and then Discover. This card exists because this screen looks broken, and it is not — it is simply showing you nothing yet. Let’s read it together, piece by piece.

A sign-in screen? That is card 4, not a fault

Type lab_kibana and LabKibana001, press Log in, and carry on. The browser will not ask again.

Do this

  1. Click the blue Search entire time range button in the middle of the screen (marker 5). That is it — one click and your records appear.
  2. Check the Data view control on the far left of the search bar says auth-*. It does, and that is the one you want.
Do not click “Try ES|QL” — here is what happens if you do

Newer Kibana includes ES|QL, a different query language. The Try ES|QL button is an advert for it, aimed at people who already know their way around Kibana. If you click it you will land on a screen showing a query that looks for indices called logs-* and filebeat-*.

Our lab has no such indices — it has auth-* and network-*. So the query cannot work, and the error you will see is expected. It does not mean the lab is broken, and there is nothing for you to fix.

What to do instead: press the browser’s Back button to return to the screen above, then carry on. This guide only ever uses the KQL search bar.

So what is wrong right now?

Exactly one thing: the time range. The data view is right, the search bar is right, Kibana is healthy, and the 280 records are sitting in the database waiting for you. The logs are simply older than the last fifteen minutes.

That is the single most common reason a beginner meets an empty screen. The Search entire time range button fixes it for you right now; card 7 shows you how to pin an exact window by hand instead, so your counts are stable for the rest of the lab.

Pick a pile5

Choose which pile of logs to look at

which logs?2 min

First, tell Discover which pile of logs to read. There are two of yours, plus one built-in entry you should ignore, and only one of them is where this attack starts.

Do this

  1. Click the control on the far left of the search bar, the one with the label Data view beside it (marker 4 on the next picture).
  2. Look at the list. Leave auth-* selected — it already is, and it already has a tick next to it. If it is already ticked there is nothing to do.
  3. Press Esc to close the list again.

What the two data views are

Data viewMatchesHoldsDocuments
auth-*auth-*Logons, logoffs, lockouts, privilege assignment, program starts280
network-*network-*Connections between machines — background noise for this scenario140

The * is a wildcard meaning “anything starting with auth”, so one entry covers every day of auth logs. We stay in auth-* from here to the end of the lab, because this investigation lives entirely in logon records.

Why this matters more than it looks

A data view is a bookmark. It tells Kibana which pile of documents to read and which field holds the time. Pick the wrong one and a perfectly good query returns nothing at all, because the documents it is looking for are not in that pile.

So whenever a query returns zero results, check these three things in this order: the data view, then the time range, then the query itself. Nine times out of ten it is one of the first two, never the third.

If the sidebar says “0 available fields” and the drop-down is empty

Then the data views were not created properly. Do not fight it — run setup-lab.cmd again. It is safe to run twice, it reloads nothing, and it now verifies each data view and tells you plainly if anything is wrong instead of printing a hopeful message.

Be precise6

Set the time range to the right day

pin an exact window4 min

Your data is loaded and the right data view is selected. Pinning the day by hand instead of using “entire time range” is what makes every count in the rest of this guide come out exactly as printed.

Do this

  1. Look at the right of the search bar. There are two date buttons side by side, joined by an arrow. The left one is the start, the right one is the end. Click the left one.
  2. A panel opens with three tabs: Absolute, Relative, Now. Absolute is already selected — it is the only one that lets you type a date. The panel shows a calendar for September 2026 and a column of half-hourly times.
  3. At the bottom of the panel, in the box labelled Start date, select the text and type exactly Sep 22, 2026 @ 00:00:00.000. Underneath the box it lists the formats it accepts.
  4. Click the blue tick to the right of that box, or just press Enter. The panel closes and the start date is set.
  5. Now click the right-hand date button, and do the same with the box labelled End date, typing Sep 22, 2026 @ 23:59:59.999. Tick it again.
  6. Look at the button on the far right of the search bar. It now says Update instead of Refresh. Click Update to apply the new range.
Check yourself against these three, before you type a query
  • The two date buttons read Sep 22, 2026 @ 00:00:00.000 and Sep 22, 2026 @ 23:59:59.999.
  • The tab reads Documents (280).
  • The sidebar reads 18 available fields and 4 meta fields, with the field names listed underneath.

If all three match, you are in the right place and the rest of the lab’s numbers will match too. If any of them does not, stop and fix it now rather than carrying a wrong time window through six queries.

The one thing that will look “wrong”: Kibana prints times in your timezone

This trips up almost everyone, so read it before you go further.

The timestamps in this lab are stored in UTC. But the @timestamp column, the histogram, and the friendly dates inside a document all follow your computer’s timezone, and no setting in the time picker changes that. If your machine is 8 hours ahead of UTC, the successful logon this guide calls 03:15:00.000 appears in your table as 11:15:00.000.

Every picture in this guide was taken with the display timezone set to UTC, so the times you see in them are the true stored values. Here is the rule that keeps you out of trouble:

  • Read the clock times off your own screen and write down what you see. Your timeline will be internally consistent, which is all a timeline needs.
  • Trust the gaps, not the absolute numbers. Every conclusion in this guide is about how far apart things are, and a timezone shift moves every time by the same amount. The gaps here — 2 minutes, 2 minutes, … then 17 minutes — are identical in every timezone.
  • The raw value never shifts. Inside an expanded document the original ISO string is shown exactly as stored, with its Z: that one is always 2026-09-22T03:15:00.000Z, on every machine, forever.
  • If you want the screen to match these pictures exactly, the simplest fix is to set your computer’s timezone to UTC before you start. Not required — but then nothing in the rest of this guide will look out of place.
Remember this one, and it will save you hours

An empty screen in Kibana is almost never a broken query. It is almost always the time range or the data view. Check those two first, every time.

And beware: if you ever press F5 to reload, or wander off to another page and come back, the time range snaps back to Last 15 minutes and the screen goes empty again. That is not your fault and it is not broken — just repeat this card. Some analysts keep the working Discover tab open in a bookmark for exactly this reason.

Why this matters

Every single stage of this attack happened on one day: 22 September 2026. A time window even slightly too narrow hides the evidence silently, and you would conclude, wrongly, that nothing happened at all. This is also why the guide quotes whole-day numbers: with the day pinned, Documents (280) is your control total, and any later query returning more than 280 means you typed the query wrong, not that you found a surprise.

Investigate7

Query 1 — the baseline

1 of 6 queries2 min

First we look at everything, to see the normal shape of a normal day. Every later query narrows this down, so this first one is your reference point.

Why you are running this query

You have 280 log records and no idea which ones matter. This query throws away the 16 records that are not account activity, so what is left is just the account activity: logons, failures, logoffs, lockouts, privilege assignments. That becomes your baseline — the “normal” you compare everything else against.

Without a baseline you cannot spot an anomaly, because you would have nothing to say what normal looked like.

Do this

Click inside the search bar, select whatever is there, and type exactly this — including the double quotes — then press Enter:

Type this into the search bar, then press Enterevent.category: "authentication"
What you should see

The Documents tab changes to Documents (264) and the table fills with rows. Each row is one account event, newest first.

What that number tells you

264 account events happened that day, in total. That is the size of the haystack you are about to search. It is also your control total — if a later query gives a number bigger than 264, you have made a mistake in the query, not found a surprise.

Why this matters

This is your baseline. The attacker is somewhere inside those 264 records, and the job for the rest of the guide is to carve them out. Never skip a baseline — without it you cannot say what “normal” looked like, and so you cannot say what was abnormal.

The dead end8

Query 2 — every failed logon, and nothing to show for it

2 of 6 queriesa deliberate dead end

Now narrow from “all account activity” to the part the alert is about: logons that failed. This card is deliberately unsatisfying, and the reason it is unsatisfying is the lesson.

Type this, then press Enterevent.code: 4625
What you should see

The tab reads Documents (66). Write that number down — it is the day’s total noise level, and it is not your answer.

Now ask: how many different things are these?

Click the Field statistics tab, just to the right of Documents (66). It lists one row per field, with how many documents have it and how many distinct values it contains. Three rows matter here, and they are at the bottom of the list, so scroll the table down.

What those two numbers tell you — and what they do not

66 failures is not evidence of anything. They are spread over 20 accounts and 5 addresses, and the biggest share of any single account is a handful of rows. That is what a normal day of mistyped passwords looks like. The 46 failures that did not come from the alert’s address are all ordinary employees typing their password wrongly.

So you have learned something important: this alert is not provable from failure counts alone. You have to isolate a single source address — and the histogram above is a good hint that the early hours are worth a look.

Why the guide makes you do a useless query on purpose

Because this is the mistake almost every beginner makes first, and making it here is cheaper than making it on a live incident at 3 a.m. The instinct is “the alert says failed logons, so let me look at the failed logons” — and 66 rows of ordinary noise is what you get. You cannot investigate “the failed logons”. You have to narrow to a source. The next card does exactly that, and it takes one more keystroke.

The breakthrough9

Query 3 — the failures from the one address in the alert

3 of 6 queriesthe finding

Add one clause and the noise disappears. This is the same single query the companion brief instructions.md gives you as its one-shot investigation query, so if you only ever run one query in this lab, run this one.

Type this, then press Enter -- keep both sets of quotesevent.code: 4625 and source.ip: "203.0.113.45"

The two clauses mean:

  • event.code: 4625 — keep only “an account failed to log on”.
  • source.ip: "203.0.113.45" — keep only the ones that came from the external address named in the alert. Type the quotes.
  • and — both must be true.
What you should see

The tab reads Documents (20), the histogram collapses to two bars in the early hours, and the sidebar gains a Selected fields  4 group because we are about to add columns. Write the number down: 20.

Now add the four columns that make the pattern visible

Click the Columns button at the right of the tab bar (marker 9), tick @timestamp, user.name, host.name and source.ip, and close the panel. Then click the @timestamp heading until the arrow points up, so the oldest attempt is the first row.

The finding you have just earned
  • 20 attempts, 20 distinct usernames. One attempt per account, so the count of rows and the count of names are the same number. Nobody was tried twice.
  • One destination host, sec-win-01. The whole walk was aimed at a single server.
  • A constant two-minute gap for 38 minutes, from 02:20 to 02:58. No human types passwords on a 120-second metronome; a script does, and a script is walking a list.
  • 13 of the 20 names are obvious guesses — admin, root, test, backup, sql, oracle, web, sysadmin, service, svc, helpdesk, finance, hr. The other 7 are real corporate usernames. That split is the proof this is a list of guesses against a known estate, not random spraying.

No account was ever under pressure, which is why no lockout alarm fired and why this ran for 38 minutes unnoticed. Card 13 proves that absence.

What a suspicious answer looks like, versus a benign one

Suspicious: a different account on every row, one destination host, identical time gaps, from an outside address. Benign: the same account failing several times in a burst — that is a real person, or a real brute force, and it normally ends in a lockout.

The payoff10

Query 4 — what that same address managed to log on as

4 of 6 queriesthis is the incident
Why you are running the next query

The enumeration was the preparation. Twenty failed logons is noise. Twenty failed logons followed by one success from the same address is a confirmed compromise of one account, and it is the only thing in this lab that changes the verdict from “close it” to “escalate it”.

Type this, then press Enter -- note the code is 4624, not 4625event.code: 4624 and source.ip: "203.0.113.45"

4624 is the event id for “an account was successfully logged on”. It is a one-character difference from 4625 and it is the single most important keystroke in this lab.

What you should see

The tab reads Documents (1). One row. Open it with the expand button (the two diagonal arrows left of the timestamp), then type message into the panel’s Search field names or values box so the one field you care about is on screen.

The finding — and the link you have to make deliberately
  • The account is administrator — the Windows built-in administrative account. It cannot be renamed, often cannot be locked out, and frequently survives with a weak or default password. It is a prized target.
  • It is already in your Query 3 list. Go back and look: administrator is the second name in the walk. The attacker probed it, decided it was real, and came back. That is the whole chain, in one glance.
  • Same host. sec-win-01 again — the very server that was being probed. No second machine, no new target.
  • 17 minutes later. The last probe was 02:58:00.000; the success is 03:15:00.000. The gap is short enough to be the same session of work and long enough to be a deliberate return.
  • Two records, all day. Search the whole day for that account and you will find exactly two events: the one failure at 02:22 and this one success. Nothing else it did is in the log — which means you have found the compromise, and you have not found any follow-on activity yet.

Write down the account name exactly as it appears. It goes in your report, and it is the pivot for every remaining query.

The most common way to fail this lab

Stopping at the failed logons and writing “20 failed logons, no breach”. Twenty failed logons really is nothing much on its own. The successful logon is the incident. A report that omits it is incomplete, however beautifully the rest of it is written.

Prove it11

Query 5 — the wrong pivot, on purpose

5 of 6 queries34 is not 20
Why you are running a query you already know is wrong

Go back to the host you found in card 10 and look at all of its failures. This is the query a beginner runs first, and running it here is cheaper than running it on a live incident. It is the check that separates a lucky analyst from a good one.

Type this, then press Enterevent.code: 4625 and host.name: "sec-win-01"

Every clause is correct and every value is real — sec-win-01 is the host you read off the host.name column in card 10, character for character. The query is still the wrong way to ask the question. That is the point of the card.

What you should see

The tab reads Documents (34). That is not 20. Put the two numbers side by side: 20 from the address, 34 from the host. 14 extra rows appeared the moment you changed the pivot. Those 14 are the point of the card.

So which number goes in your report? Neither, on its own

34 is not the attacker’s activity, and 20 is not the host’s activity. They are two different questions. The report has to say which question it is answering every time it quotes a number, and the second most common mistake in this exercise is quoting the host total (34) as though it were the attacker’s (20).

Why the target host is the noisiest place to look

Because the host being probed is also collecting ordinary mistyped passwords from other people all day. Anyone who fat-fingers their password against sec-win-01 lands in your results, forever, mixed in with the attacker.

The address is the signal; the host is only the target. Knowing which pivot to use — and being able to show why the other one misleads you — is a core analyst skill, and it is exactly what this card is for.

Prove it12

Query 6 — the lockout that never happened

6 of 6 queriesan absence as evidence
Why you are looking for something that is not there

Windows locks an account after enough failures — event 4740. A brute-force attack trips it and gets itself noticed. If an attacker can walk twenty accounts without tripping it once, that is not luck: it is deliberate pacing, and a good report says so explicitly.

First, prove that lockouts exist at all today

Never report an absence before you have shown the thing can appear. Run this first:

Search A -- every lockout on the estate, all dayevent.code: 4740

The tab should read Documents (24). Lockouts are not rare in this estate, so a zero in the next query cannot be explained away as “the lab has no lockout records”.

Now ask the question that matters

Add the attacker’s address to the same query:

Search B -- lockouts caused by the enumerating addressevent.code: 4740 and source.ip: "203.0.113.45"
What you should see: nothing at all

Zero matches. Kibana does not draw a Documents tab when there is nothing to count, so you get the No results match your search criteria panel instead. Both are the same answer, and this is the answer: no lockouts from that address, all day, while it walked twenty accounts.

Why the absence is stronger evidence than a presence

Anyone can find a row that exists. Proving a row is missing takes a control — and you have one: 24 lockouts elsewhere on the same day, none of them from this address. So the attacker did not merely fail to trip a lockout; they avoided one, deliberately, across twenty accounts and 38 minutes, by never trying the same account twice.

Write that sentence into your report. It is the difference between describing an incident and explaining one.

The bonus13

Read the rejection status — how the list became knowledge

the cleverest finding in the lab

One quick step, and it is the most interesting thing in the dataset. It explains why the attacker walked a list at all, instead of spraying passwords at one account.

Do this

  1. Re-run card 10’s query so the twenty probes are on screen again.
  2. Click the expand button — the two diagonal arrows immediately left of the timestamp, on the first row.
  3. In the panel’s Search field names or values box, type message. The panel narrows to that one field.
  4. Read the message value from left to right, and stop at the Status: at the end. Press Esc, open the second row the same way, and compare.
The Status you seeWhat Windows means by itWhat the attacker learned
0xC0000064“no such user” — the name does not existNothing. A wrong guess. Move on.
0xC000006A“wrong password” — the account is realA valid username, harvested without ever guessing a password.
What the twenty statuses add up to
StatusHow many of the 20 probesMeaning
0xC000006413The name does not exist. The attacker guessed wrong and moved on.
0xC000006A7The account is real. A valid-username list, harvested for free.

The seven real names are administrator, jdoe, asmith, mchen, kpatel, rneuman and svega. Every one of them is a name you can see logging in normally elsewhere in the day — they are colleagues. And one of the seven is the account that was compromised.

Why this is the finding that makes the whole thing click

Compare the two populations. The 46 failures from other addresses that day — your colleagues mistyping — are 100% 0xC000006A, because a real employee’s account exists and only the password was wrong. The attacker’s failures are 65% 0xC0000064, because they were guessing at names that mostly do not exist.

So the log itself carries the attacker’s feedback channel. They were not spraying; they were querying the directory through the authentication service, one name at a time, reading a one-bit answer each time, and building a clean list of valid usernames without ever guessing a password twice against the same account and therefore without ever tripping a lockout.

That is why the walk took 38 minutes instead of 38 seconds, and why it was invisible. And it is the answer to the question a manager will ask you: if they only got one password right at the very end, how did they know who to try? They did not guess. They asked, twenty times, and the server told them.

Put it together14

Build the timeline

most important 5 min

This is the most important 5 minutes in the lab. Investigators do not just collect facts — they arrange them so the facts argue the conclusion for them.

Do this

Open a text file (Notepad is fine) and write four lines, oldest first, using the timestamps you found. Then run this one last search, which is the whole story on a single screen: the attacker’s address, both event codes, and a window tight around the run.

Type this, then set the time range to 02:10 - 03:25 on the same daysource.ip: "203.0.113.45" and (event.code: 4625 or event.code: 4624)

Set the time range with the left date button to Sep 22, 2026 @ 02:10:00.000 and the right one to Sep 22, 2026 @ 03:25:00.000, tick both, then click Update. The tab should read Documents (21) — twenty probes and one success, nothing else.

  1. 02:20:00.000 → 02:58:00.000
    20 failed logons (4625) from 203.0.113.45, one per distinct account, all against sec-win-01, at a constant two-minute interval. No lockout.
  2. 02:22:00.000 — inside that run
    The account administrator is probed and comes back Status: 0xC000006A — wrong password, so the account is real.
  3. + 17 minutes of silence
    Nothing at all from that address. The 17-minute gap between the last probe and the next event is itself a fact.
  4. 03:15:00.000
    1 successful logon (4624) for the same account from the same address, on the same host as sec-win-01.
The shape of the answer

All four stages fall inside a 55-minute window on a single day, and the attack itself took 17 minutes from first probe to compromise. Nothing is hours apart, nothing is days apart. This tightness is itself evidence — it rules out coincidence and routine administration.

Then ask the four questions that turn facts into a verdict

QuestionYour answer comes from
Who started it?source.ip = 203.0.113.45 — an address outside your 10.0.4.0/24 range
What did they take?the built-in administrator account, on sec-win-01
How did they get in?20 one-per-account probes, reading the rejection status, then 1 success
How far did they get?one host, one account. No second machine appears anywhere in the log.
The one-sentence verdict

Between 02:20 and 03:15 UTC on 22 September 2026, the external address 203.0.113.45 walked a list of 20 usernames against the server sec-win-01 at a constant two-minute interval, reading each rejection to learn which accounts existed — 13 did not, 7 did — never triggering a lockout, and then successfully authenticated as the built-in administrator account seventeen minutes after the last probe.

That is a true positive, and every clause of that sentence is traceable to one of the six queries you just ran.

Write the report, then prove it

25 mindo not skip

Nobody reads your screen. This card is the deliverable — it is the thing you hand in, and it is the only place in the guide you type. It has two parts and both go into your submission: Part one is your written report, Part two is the set of figures you checked off your own screen as you went. Neither part has an answer printed next to it. Fill both in, then press EXPORT MY SUBMISSION at the bottom: a finished PDF report lands in your Downloads folder with your name and batch number on the front of it.

Do this yourself, and do it now

If you cannot fill a line in without going back to Kibana, you have not finished the investigation — which is exactly the point. These fields are deliberately empty and stay that way until you type. Nothing here is marked against a model answer; it is marked on whether you found these things.

Both of these are printed at the top of the exported PDF and go into the file name, so the submission is identifiable without you having to say who you are in the report itself. Leave either one blank and the file still exports — it just says [not answered] where your name should be, which is a good reason not to leave them blank.

Part one — your report

1. Summary

What happened

two or three sentences a manager could follow, and no jargon in the first sentence

2. Timeline

When

one line per stage, oldest first, with the times read off your own screen — not off this guide. Card 15 is the timeline card that builds it

3. Evidence

How you know

each query you ran, the number it returned, and what that number proved. The number matters as much as the reasoning

4. Impact

What is affected

the account that was taken over, every account the attacker identified as real, and the server that was probed

5. Verdict

True positive or false positive

state it plainly in the first line, then the whole chain in one paragraph

6. Recommendations

What should happen next

concrete actions in the order you would carry them out. If a change has to be made twice to actually work, say so — that is the single most-missed step in a response, and the words card explains what it is called

Part two — the figures behind it

Every line below is a number you should be able to point at on your own screen. These travel with your report, so a figure that contradicts your writing gives you away — if Part one and Part two disagree, one of them is wrong, and you want to know which before you hand it in.

Three things worth double-checking in your own report

These are the three that catch people out, so read yours back now:

  1. Did you narrow to the source address? A report that stops at “event.code: 4625 returned a lot of rows, and failed logons look normal” is incomplete. The event code on its own is not a finding — you had to add a source address before the picture appeared.
  2. Did you quote 20, or 34? 34 is the host total and includes 14 unrelated failures from four other addresses; 20 is the attacker total. Reporting the host number as the attacker's is the single most common mistake in this lab, and card 12 exists to catch it.
  3. Did you run the 4624 query at all? The failed logons are noise until the success proves they were preparation. A report that never runs it is incomplete, however good the rest of it reads.

And one bonus: if you wrote down that the seven “real accounts” the attacker harvested are all now targeted, and not just the one that was taken over, say so in your report. It is not required, and nothing checks it automatically, but it is the sentence that turns a list of counts into a response.

Export it

Anything you left blank is written in as [not answered] rather than quietly dropped, so a hole cannot turn into a tidy-looking submission. The PDF lands in your Downloads folder; nothing is uploaded and no internet connection is needed.

Clean up16

Double-click teardown.cmd

leave no trace1 min

Finished. Now remove the lab completely. This matters: the lab stores its data in a Docker volume, and volumes are not removed when you close a window or shut down your computer. Left behind, it silently occupies disk space until someone deletes it by hand.

Do this

  1. Open the lab folder again.
  2. On Windows, find teardown.cmd and double-click it.
    On macOS or Linux, run ./teardown.sh instead.
  3. It lists exactly what it is about to remove, and asks you to confirm.
  4. Press Y and Enter. That is the whole process.

What it deletes — and what it does not

ObjectNameWhy
Containeraccount-enumeration-001-elasticsearchThe database process
Containeraccount-enumeration-001-kibanaThe website process
Networkaccount-enumeration-001_labThe private network they shared
Volumeaccount-enumeration-001_esdataAll 420 log documents and the detection rule — the disk space
Folder%TEMP%\elklab-account-enumeration-001Temporary files the setup made
What it deliberately keeps
  • The Elasticsearch and Kibana images. These are the big downloads — over a gigabyte. Keeping them means the next time you run this lab, setup-lab.cmd starts in under a minute instead of twenty.
  • Everything else on your computer. Other Docker projects, other labs, your images, your other volumes — all untouched.

Every object name above begins with this lab’s own folder name. That is not a coincidence — it is how the script guarantees it can only ever delete its own lab, and nothing else on your machine. If the folder had been moved or renamed, the names would have changed with it.

What you should see

The last thing the teardown file prints Removing... compose down -v completed Verifying... gone container account-enumeration-001-elasticsearch gone container account-enumeration-001-kibana gone volume account-enumeration-001_esdata gone network account-enumeration-001_lab gone file .../docker-compose.yml gone folder %TEMP%\elklab-account-enumeration-001 ============================================================== The "account-enumeration-001" lab has been removed. Kept on purpose: every Docker image, and every other container and volume on this machine.

That Verifying block is the honest one. The script checks every object after removing it and prints what it actually finds, so a second run says Nothing to remove and Lab state : already clean rather than claiming to have deleted something that was never there. If anything genuinely could not be removed you will see a line beginning WARNING, and the closing block will say Partly removed instead of has been removed.

Want to check it really worked?

Open Docker Desktop and look under Volumes (or run docker volume ls). There should be no account-enumeration-001_esdata entry. The containers are gone from Containers too. If either is still listed, run teardown.cmd again — it is safe to run as many times as you like, and it says what it actually did each time.

If Docker is not running when you do this, the script cannot delete containers or volumes. It will say so plainly, clean what it can, and tell you exactly what is left rather than pretending.

Why bother?

Two reasons, and the second is the important one.

Practical: a lab volume is real disk space, and a machine with a dozen abandoned lab volumes will eventually run out of room or fail to start new containers. Cleaning up is part of being a professional.

Discipline: an analyst who leaves environments running on a shared or corporate machine causes real problems — port conflicts, someone else’s lab failing to start, resources nobody knows are being used. Leave it as you found it is a habit worth forming now, before anyone is paying you for it.

Reference⚙

If something goes wrong

keep this open

Almost every problem in this lab is one of five things. Check them in this order before assuming the worst.

The query returns nothing

  • Check the time range. This is the cause nine times out of ten. It should read Sep 22, 2026 @ 00:00:00.000 – Sep 22, 2026 @ 23:59:59.999. Reloading the page resets it to the last 15 minutes.
  • Check the data view is auth-*, not All logs and not network-*. If the dropdown is empty, re-run setup-lab.cmd.
  • Check the quotes were typed exactly as shown. A missing " around an address silently changes what the query means.
  • Check the code. 4625 is a failure, 4624 is a success, 4740 is a lockout. Reading 4,625 off the screen is the same value as 4625 — the screen just adds a thousands separator.
  • Getting zero results is sometimes the answer, not a fault. Card 13 relies on it. Before you go hunting, ask whether you expected results at all.

The sidebar says “0 available fields” and “18 empty fields”

  • This is not a broken data view. It means “this data view has 18 fields, but none of them hold data inside the time range you have selected”.
  • Widen the time range (card 7) and Available fields will replace Empty fields, and the field names will appear.
  • Only if Empty fields is showing a number of 0 as well is something actually wrong — then re-run setup-lab.cmd.

The sidebar says “18 available fields” but the table is empty

  • That combination means your query matches nothing inside the time range. The field list counts fields in the data view; the results count what matched.
  • Check the query box really contains what you think — there is a × button at its right end that clears it in one click.

The counts are wrong

  • Not Documents (280) on the auth-* view? You may be on network-* (140 documents) or on All logs, or your time range is narrower than the whole day.
  • Much larger than 280? The data was loaded twice. Run setup-lab.cmd reset — that is clean and guaranteed to fix it. The setup script will refuse to import on top of a partial load, so this can only happen if you imported by hand.
  • Seeing a “Create a data view” box instead of Discover? You are in Stack Management, not Discover. Use the ☰ menu at the top left and choose Discover.

Elasticsearch or Kibana will not start

  • Is Docker Desktop running? It must be, and it must say Engine running. This is the cause almost every time.
  • Ports. Elasticsearch wants 9200, Kibana wants 5601. If another program already owns either, stop it.
  • Be patient. A cold start that downloads over a gigabyte and then shows nothing for several minutes is normal, not hung. The script prints a stage number at each step and dumps the last 40 log lines if something times out.
  • Open http://localhost:9200 in a browser. A short JSON reply naming Elasticsearch means the database is healthy and the problem is Kibana — which takes noticeably longer to become ready.
  • Do not install your own Elasticsearch or Kibana. You do not need them; the lab starts its own copies inside Docker.
  • Another lab is already on port 9200? The setup script refuses to touch it and tells you the cluster name it found. Stop that lab, or change ESPORT at the top of the file and run setup-lab.cmd regen-compose.

The screen does not look like the picture

  • Compare the words, not the pixels. These are real screenshots, so every label in the picture is genuinely on your screen. What can differ is how much room each thing gets: a wider window shows more columns, a narrower one wraps text and may push a control onto a second line. Same words, different layout.
  • Your clock times will differ if you are not on UTC. Card 7 explains the rule: trust the gaps, not the absolute numbers.
  • Stuck in a panel you cannot leave? Press Esc.
Still stuck?

Write down exactly what you clicked, what you expected, and what happened instead, then ask your instructor. That description is the skill — being able to report a problem precisely is most of a real analyst’s job.

Stuck on a step?

Almost every problem in this lab has one of five causes, and all five are covered on the If something goes wrong card near the end: the time range reset, the wrong data view, a mistyped quote, a 4624 typed as 4625, or Docker not running. Go there rather than guessing.
